What an Attacker Can Do With XSS
Depends entirely on the specific XSS type found and the attacker's actual goal:
Pure defacement: Integrity is heavily hit, Confidentiality and Availability largely untouched
Full account takeover: all three (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) can be affected

XSS with other bugs or with functionality normally reserved for privileged users to escalate impact dramatically — a real example cited: a Magento vulnerability where a stored XSS bug was chained into arbitrary code execution.
XSS had its own dedicated OWASP Top 10 category in 2010, 2013, and 2017, but in the most recent list it was folded into the broader "Injection" category — currently the

most critical risk facing web applications. In direct testing experience: essentially every application tested has had at least one XSS vulnerability somewhere — it remains extremely common despite the long history of known defenses.

How to Find and Exploit XSS Vulnerabilities
— any decent scanner should reliably catch most

XSS, since it's comparatively mechanical to detect. Stored and DOM-based XSS are harder for scanners — some catch them, some miss them — so manual verification alongside an automated scan is standard practice, not optional. Burp Suite Pro is the personal preference cited, though free/open-source options exist across a range of budgets.
Encode all user-controllable data at the point of output, before it's rendered — this ensures it's displayed as inert
, never interpreted as executable code. The correct encoding is

: HTML encoding for data inserted into HTML, JavaScript encoding for data inserted into a script context, and so on — a single encoding scheme doesn't cover every context an application might reflect input into. Never hand-roll an encoding routine (same rule as with crypto) — use a well-established library for your language/framework; OWASP maintains a list of recommended options per stack.
Primary Defense — Input Validation on Arrival
Only accept input matching what's actually expected for that field — e.g. an age field should accept integers only, nothing else. An
is always more secure than a denylist, but a denylist is sometimes unavoidable in practice — which is exactly why input filtering is classified as a
layer rather than a complete standalone defense: a denylist is inherently incomplete against a sufficiently creative payload.

tell the browser what format a response actually is. Set correctly, they stop a browser from executing injected HTML/JS on a response that was never meant to be interpreted as such. Doesn't apply everywhere — many pages legitimately need to serve HTML/JS — so this is a supplementary layer, not the official defense.
Defense in Depth — Content Security Policy (CSP)
A browser-enforced mechanism restricting what resources a page is allowed to load and whether the page can be framed by others (relevant to both XSS and clickjacking). Configured via the

response header, containing one or more semicolon-separated directives. A strict example policy might allow images/scripts/AJAX/CSS only from the page's own origin and nothing else — under that policy, a script an attacker tries to load from their own server simply won't execute, since it isn't same-origin. CSP is powerful but genuinely deep enough to be its own topic; treat it as the last line of defense, not the first thing to reach for.
: output encoding and input validation on arrival are the two things you should always be doing; response headers and CSP are valuable additional layers on top, not substitutes for the first two.
